title: Parallel Broyden methods for efficiently evaluating nonlinear state space models
claim: Our quasi-Newton method needs fewer iterations than diagonal approximations and wins on runtime when Jacobian evaluation is expensive, with rank trading iterations for time.
layout: 2x3 grid of line plots, shared legend on top, columns are settings
description: A 2x3 grid of line plots under a single horizontal legend. The legend lists Sequential (green), Newton (red), Diag. Quasi-Newton (orange), Parallel Broyden (blue triangles, bold) and Accelerated Parallel Broyden (purple inverted triangles, bold). Columns are a standard low-rank RNN, a low-rank MLP-RNN, and a full-rank DMF RNN. The top row shows the number of fixed-point iterations on a log scale. The bottom row shows wallclock time in seconds on a log scale. The left and middle columns vary sequence length T from 10^3 to 10^5, and the right column varies Broyden rank m from 0 to 80. Shaded bands show interquartile ranges. In the right column, the methods without a rank parameter appear as flat horizontal lines. The eye goes first to the blue and purple dashed curves, which sit between orange and red in iterations. In the right column they show iterations falling and runtime rising as rank increases.
caption: Low-rank and full-rank RNNs. Left, middle: Standard (∆t = 0.5) and MLP (∆t = 3) low-rank RNNs (R = 3, D = 200), as T varies. In both, iteration counts are ordered as diagonal quasi-Newton > Parallel Broyden > Accelerated Parallel Broyden > Newton. This ordering translates into runtime only when Jacobian information is expensive (MLP-RNN). Right: Full-rank DMF RNN (D = 128, T = 104) as the Broyden rank m varies. Methods without a rank parameter are shown as horizontal lines. Accelerated Parallel Broyden is shown only up to m = 20, as for larger m it becomes numerically unstable or fails to converge. Larger m reduces iterations but increases runtime. We report median iteration counts and runtimes with interquartile ranges over 32 random realizations. Runtimes are computed over realizations that converged within the 1000 iterations budget.
abstract: Nonlinear state space models are typically evaluated sequentially, limiting their ability to exploit modern parallel hardware. Recent work has shown that state space models can be evaluated in parallel by reformulating evaluation as a root-finding problem, which can be solved with a parallel form of Newton's method. However, exact Newton methods require expensive multiplication of dense Jacobian matrices, and quasi-Newton methods based on diagonal approximations, while more scalable, are often slow to converge because they neglect interactions across state dimensions. We introduce a novel quasi-Newton approach based on Broyden's method, which captures coupling terms with diagonal-plus-low-rank approximations to blocks of the Jacobian. We construct the approximations from trajectory secants, avoiding automatic differentiation while retaining the favorable scaling of diagonal approximations and remaining compatible with parallel scan through rank compression. We prove finite-step recovery of the exact trajectory under the compressed scan, and show that convergence is tracked by the compression error and by the block approximation error along the current trajectory error, rather than in spectral norm. Empirically, we show that our method is advantageous when interactions are approximately low rank or when Jacobian evaluation is expensive: on low-rank RNNs, parallel MCMC algorithms, and denoising diffusion models, it converges in fewer iterations than other quasi-Newton methods and is the fastest parallel method when Jacobian evaluation is expensive or state dimensions are large.
